newsitem.title: GERMANY: LAWYERS SEEK SUSPENDED SENTENCE FOR GRAF'S FATHER.
newsitem.headline: LAWYERS SEEK SUSPENDED SENTENCE FOR GRAF'S FATHER.

text.p: Defence lawyers on Monday requested a suspended sentence and a fine for the father of tennis star Steffi Graf, whose trial for evading millions of marks of tax on his daughter's earnings is due to end this week.

Lawyers for Peter Graf do not deny that their client set out to evade up to six million marks ($3.7 million) of tax on his daughter's earnings -- less than a third of the sum alleged by the prosecution.
But they said Peter Graf's own naivety, the negligence of his tax advisers and the authorities' failure to act much earlier all contributed to the situation he now faced.
The advisers' idea of using tax havens abroad to conceal the world number one woman player's earnings was idiocy, "but no one told Peter Graf", defence lawyer Kurt Himmelsbach said.
If the tax authorities had done their duty by acting three years earlier, Peter Graf, 58, and co-accused, Joachim Eckardt, 49, an adviser, would "have got off with a black eye", he added.
Prosecutors say Graf and Eckardt concealed 19.2 million marks ($11.8 million at current exchange rates) of Steffi Graf's earnings from German authorities between 1989 and 1993.
They have demanded a sentence of six years and nine months for Graf, and four years and nine months for Eckardt.
The court's verdict will be announced on Friday along with any sentence.
Himmelsbach asked the court for a sentence short enough to be suspended, which means no more than two years, and offered the payment of a fine to reduce the length of the prison term.

Graf's lawyers argued during the five-month trial that he was a weak man, out of his depth, who had been led astray. They have cited an addiction to alcohol and tablets, and traumas including a highly publicised affair with a call girl.
But they apppeared to differ on Friday on the extent to which he could actually be held responsible for his actions.
Himmelsbach, the Grafs' old family lawyer, said he disagreed with a report from a court-appointed psychiatrist which said Graf was fully responsible.
But celebrity lawyer Franz Salditt intervened to say that "with Peter Graf's express approval, I consider the report correct. There's no such thing as a compulsion to find ways to avoid paying tax".
A penitent Graf, who spent 16 months in custody before being released on bail, told the court: "I will never forget this trial as long as I live, and I don't want to forget it."

Steffi Graf could in theory be at home in Germany for the conclusion of the trial, after she unexpectedly lost in the fourth round of the Australian Open. The loss ended a record run of 45 matches without defeat in the four major Grand Slam events. ($1=1.6285 Mark)
